claims.text: Over 1,300 Stripe pull requests merged each week are completely minion-produced (up from 1,000 as of Part 1), human-reviewed, and contain no human-written code.
Over a thousand pull requests merged each week at Stripe were completely minion-produced as of Part 1, human-reviewed, with no human-written code.
A typical minion run starts in a Slack message and ends in a pull request that passes CI and is ready for human review, with no interaction in between.
Minions run in isolated devboxes, the same type of machine Stripe engineers write code on.
Devboxes are pre-warmed so one can be spun up in 10 seconds, with Stripe code and services pre-loaded.
Devboxes are isolated from production resources and the internet, so minions can run on them without human permission checks.
Devbox isolation gives parallelization without the overhead of git worktrees, which wouldn't scale at Stripe.
A Stripe devbox is an AWS EC2 instance containing Stripe's source code and running services under development.
Because mistakes are confined to the blast radius of one devbox, the agent runs with full permissions and without confirmation prompts.
Minions are fully unattended, so the harness cannot use human-facing features such as interruptibility or human-triggered commands to steer the run.
Devbox instances are treated as cattle: identical and disposable, drawn from a pool provisioned ahead of time with repos cloned, caches warm and background services started.
The core agent loop runs on a fork of Block's coding agent goose.
Blueprints are workflows defined in code in which each node runs either deterministic code or an agent loop focused on a task.
Agent nodes in the minion blueprint, such as 'Implement task' and 'Fix CI failures', are given wide latitude to make their own decisions.
Deterministic nodes in the minion blueprint, such as 'Run configured linters' and 'Push changes', invoke no LLM and just run code.
The minion blueprint resembles a state machine intermixing deterministic code nodes and free-flowing agent nodes.
Minions connect to MCP to gather context such as internal documentation, ticket details, build statuses and Sourcegraph code intelligence.
Almost all agent rules at Stripe are conditionally applied based on subdirectories, since many unconditional rules would be impractical.
A subset of linters runs as a deterministic node, looped on locally before the branch is pushed, so the branch has a fair chance of passing CI the first time.
Local lint finishes in under 5 seconds, before any CI push.
CI selectively runs tests from a battery of over three million tests upon a push.
Many tests have autofixes for failures, which are applied automatically; failures without an autofix are sent back to the minion.
CI is limited to at most two rounds because CI runs cost tokens, compute and time.
After the second push and CI run, the branch is sent back to its human operator for manual scrutiny.

After the run, the minion pushes a branch and prepares a pull request following Stripe's PR template; the engineer requests review from another engineer, or gives the minion further instructions, which are pushed to the branch.
